lessons.title: Introduction to the Potter's Wheel
lessons.body: A potter's wheel is a simple machine: a heavy disc that spins so you can shape clay with your hands. In Africa, you'll find two main types: the traditional kick wheel (you push a heavy stone or concrete flywheel with your foot) and the electric wheel (a motor turns the head at 0â240 volts, common in cities). For a beginner, an electric wheel with a 30â40 cm head is easiest. You also need a stool that puts your hips just above the wheel head, a bucket of water, a sponge, a wire clay cutter, and a wooden rib. Clay should be wedged (kneaded) to remove air bubblesâif you don't, your pot will explode in the kiln. Use 1â2 kg of smooth stoneware or earthenware clay for your first attempts. Set your wheel speed to medium (about 100â150 rpm for centering). Sit with your elbows braced against your thighs so your hands are steady. Wet the wheel head, slam the clay ball down in the center, and press it firmly to make it stick. Never lean your whole body weight onto the spinning wheelâuse your arms and shoulders. In many African workshops, potters share one wheel, so learn to adjust the speed and seat quickly. Always keep a bucket of clean water and a sponge to lubricate the clay; too much water makes it sloppy, too little makes it drag. After throwing, clean the wheel with a sponge and scraper. Store clay in a sealed plastic bag to keep it workable. A well-maintained wheel will last decadesâoil the bearings every month if it's electric, and check the belt tension. Practice spinning an empty wheel first to get used to the motion, then try centering a small ball of clay. This is the foundation of all wheel work.

lessons.title: Centering Clay on the Wheel
lessons.body: Centering is the hardest skill in wheel throwingâif the clay is not perfectly centered, every pot will be lopsided. Start with 1 kg of wedged clay. Slam it onto the center of the wheel head and press down with your palm. Wet your hands, then turn the wheel to medium speed. Place your left hand on the left side of the clay, right hand on the right, elbows locked into your hips. Press inward and downward with the heels of your hands. The clay will wobble; keep pressure steady until it stops moving. This can take 5â10 minutes for beginners. Use a 'cone' technique: push the clay into a cone shape, then press it back down. Repeat three times. This aligns the particles and removes air pockets. Check centering by holding a finger lightly against the sideâif you feel a bump, it's off-center. Fix it by pressing harder on the high side. Water is critical: too dry, the clay tears; too wet, it slips. Dip your fingers in water, not your whole hand. In Africa, many potters use a wooden rib (a flat stick) to help press the clay evenly. Once centered, open the clay with your thumbs, pressing down into the middle, then widen the hole. Keep the wheel speed constant. If the clay starts to spiral, slow down and re-center. Centering 1 kg should take no more than 3 minutes once you're skilled. Practice with 500 g balls firstâthey're easier. Never rush; a centered ball is 80% of a good pot. After centering, you can throw a cylinder or bowl. If you fail, wedge the clay again and retry. In a shared workshop, clean the wheel between users so clay doesn't harden. Store your centered clay under plastic if you take a break.

lessons.title: Throwing Cylinders and Bowls
lessons.body: Once clay is centered, open it with your thumbs, pressing down to within 1 cm of the wheel head (don't go through). For a cylinder, widen the hole to about 3 cm, then pull the walls up. Use your left hand inside, right hand outside, both wet. Start at the base, squeeze the wall between your fingers, and pull upward slowly. Repeat 3â4 times, each time thinning the wall. Aim for a wall thickness of 5â8 mm. Keep the wheel at medium speed. If the wall gets too thin, it will collapse. For a bowl, open wider (8â10 cm) and pull the walls outward, not straight up. Use a rib to shape the curve. A good bowl has a smooth, even curve from base to rim. Throw a 1 kg cylinder to about 15 cm tall, then a 1 kg bowl to 20 cm wide. Let them dry to leather-hard (firm but still cool) before trimming. In Africa, many potters make nested bowls for serving ugali or stew. You can also throw plates: open a flat disc, then pull the rim up slightly. Always keep the rim evenâmeasure with a needle tool or your fingers. After throwing, smooth the rim with a wet sponge. If the pot wobbles, it's off-center; recenter by pressing gently. Remove the pot from the wheel with a wire cutter, sliding it under the base. Lift carefully with two hands. Place on a wooden board to dry. Cover with plastic for slow drying to prevent cracks. Practice daily: throw 10 cylinders in a row, then 10 bowls. Speed comes with muscle memory. In a shared studio, label your pots with your name. Clean your tools and wheel after each session.

lessons.title: Trimming and Finishing Wheel-Thrown Pieces
lessons.body: Trimming (also called turning) is done when the pot is leather-hardâfirm enough to hold shape but soft enough to cut. If it's too wet, it will deform; too dry, it will chip. Test by pressing a fingernail: it should leave a slight mark. You need a trimming tool (a metal loop on a handle), a chuck (a small clay mound to hold the pot upside down), and a needle tool. Center the pot upside down on the wheel head, pressing gently into the chuck. Spin the wheel slowly. Use the needle tool to mark the base's center. Then hold the trimming tool at a 45Â° angle and shave off thin layers from the base and sides. Aim for a foot ringâa raised ring on the bottom that makes the pot stable. Trim until the wall thickness is even, about 5 mm. For bowls, trim the outside curve to match the inside. Don't over-trim; stop when you see a smooth surface. After trimming, smooth the foot with a damp sponge. For finishing, you can burnish with a smooth stone or spoon to make the surface shiny. In Africa, many potters use a piece of broken gourd or a smooth river stone for burnishing. You can also add handles: roll a coil, attach with slip (clay mixed with water), and blend. Let the pot dry completely (bone dry) before firing. If you want to decorate, carve or paint with engobe (colored slip) at leather-hard stage. Always clean your tools and store them dry. Trimming is where you make a pot look professional. Practice on cylinders first, then bowls. A well-trimmed pot has a clean foot, even walls, and no cracks. If you crack a pot, recycle the clay. In a shared workshop, keep your trimming tools sharp and labeled.

lessons.title: Making Large Platters and Tiles on the Wheel
lessons.body: Large platters and tiles are thrown on the wheel using a batâa flat disc that attaches to the wheel head. You need a bat pin system or a sticky pad. For a platter, start with 2â3 kg of clay. Center it, then open a wide, flat disc, leaving a 1 cm thick base. Pull the rim outward with your fingers, keeping the wheel at low speed (50â80 rpm). Use a rib to flatten and smooth. Aim for a diameter of 30â40 cm. If the clay gets too soft, let it rest for 10 minutes, then continue. For tiles, throw a flat disc 1 cm thick, then cut it into squares or circles with a needle tool while still on the bat. Let the tile dry on the bat until leather-hard, then lift it off. In Africa, large platters are used for serving communal meals; tiles are used for floors and wall decoration. You can also make roof tiles by throwing a curved disc and cutting it. Always support large pieces with your handsâdon't let them flop. After throwing, cover with plastic and dry slowly to prevent warping. For a platter, you can add a foot ring by trimming later. If you want a perfectly flat tile, place it between two boards weighted with books while drying. Practice with 1 kg first, then increase. A common mistake is throwing too thinâlarge pieces need strength. Use a stiff clay body with grog (sand or crushed fired clay) to reduce cracking. In a shared studio, use a bat that fits your wheel head. Clean the bat after use. Fire platters and tiles slowly to avoid cracks. With practice, you can throw a 50 cm platter in 15 minutes.

lessons.title: Troubleshooting Common Wheel Throwing Problems
lessons.body: Even experienced potters face problems. Here are the most common and how to fix them. If the clay wobbles while centering, it's not centeredâstop, press harder on the high side, and re-cone. If the pot collapses, the wall is too thin or the wheel is too fast; slow down and use less water. If the rim cracks, it dried too fast; cover with plastic and slow the drying. If the base cracks, you opened too deep or didn't compress the bottom; always press the base with a sponge. If the pot is lopsided, you pulled unevenly; practice pulling with even pressure. If the clay feels sticky, it's too wet; let it dry on a plaster bat for 10 minutes. If it's too dry, dip your fingers in water. If the pot sticks to the wheel head, use a wire cutter and a little water. If you get 'S' cracks in the base, you didn't compress the clay enough after opening. If the pot has a spiral inside, you pulled too fast; slow down. In Africa, humidity affects dryingâin coastal areas, pots dry slowly; in dry regions, cover them sooner. Always wedge clay to remove air bubbles; bubbles cause explosions in the kiln. If your pot explodes, you fired too fast or had trapped air. Use a pyrometric cone to monitor temperature. For trimming problems, if the pot won't center on the chuck, use a smaller chuck or dampen the rim. If the trimming tool chatters, hold it firmly and spin slower. If you crack a pot during trimming, it's too dry; spray with water and wait. Keep a notebook of your mistakes and fixes. In a shared workshop, ask others for help. Practice each fix on scrap clay. Remember, every potter makes mistakesâthe best ones learn from them.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of wedging clay before throwing?
quiz.explanation: Wedging removes air pockets that can cause explosions in the kiln.

quiz.q: Which wheel speed is recommended for centering 1 kg of clay?
quiz.explanation: Medium speed of 100â150 rpm gives enough momentum for centering without being too fast.

quiz.q: How much clay is suggested for a beginner's first throwing attempts?
quiz.explanation: 1â2 kg is manageable for learning to center and throw without excessive fatigue.

quiz.q: What is the correct posture when throwing on the wheel?
options: B) Leaning forward with elbows on knees
C) Sitting with elbows braced against thighs
quiz.explanation: Bracing elbows against thighs keeps hands steady and prevents back strain.

quiz.q: What should you do if the clay is not centered?
options: C) Press harder on the high side
D) Start over with new clay
quiz.explanation: Pressing the high side brings the clay back to center.

quiz.q: How many times should you cone the clay during centering?
quiz.explanation: Coning three times aligns particles and removes air pockets.

quiz.q: What is the ideal wall thickness for a thrown cylinder?
quiz.explanation: 5â8 mm is strong enough to hold shape but thin enough to be elegant.

quiz.q: When throwing a bowl, how should you pull the walls?
quiz.explanation: Pulling outward creates the wide, curved shape of a bowl.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a rib in throwing?
quiz.explanation: A rib (wooden or plastic) is used to shape and compress the clay surface.

quiz.q: When is the best time to trim a pot?
quiz.explanation: Leather-hard is firm enough to hold shape but soft enough to cut cleanly.

quiz.q: What is a chuck used for in trimming?
options: A) To hold the pot upside down
quiz.explanation: A chuck is a clay mound that centers and holds the pot during trimming.

quiz.q: What is a foot ring?
options: B) A raised ring on the bottom of a pot
D) A crack in the base
quiz.explanation: A foot ring lifts the pot off the surface and adds stability.

quiz.q: What tool is used to remove a pot from the wheel?
quiz.explanation: A wire cutter slides under the base to release the pot without distorting it.

quiz.q: Why should you cover a freshly thrown pot with plastic?
options: B) To slow drying and prevent cracks
quiz.explanation: Slow, even drying prevents stress cracks.

quiz.q: What is a bat used for in wheel throwing?
options: B) To support large platters and tiles
quiz.explanation: A bat is a flat disc that attaches to the wheel head for throwing large, flat pieces.

quiz.q: What wheel speed is recommended for throwing a large platter?
quiz.explanation: Low speed gives more control and prevents the large piece from flying off.

quiz.q: What is grog used for in clay?
options: B) To reduce cracking in large pieces
quiz.explanation: Grog (sand or crushed fired clay) adds strength and reduces shrinkage cracks.

quiz.q: How should you dry a large tile to keep it flat?
options: B) Place between two boards with weight
quiz.explanation: Weighted boards prevent warping during drying.

quiz.q: What causes a pot to explode in the kiln?
options: B) Trapped air or firing too fast
quiz.explanation: Trapped air or moisture expands rapidly and shatters the pot.

quiz.q: What is the first step if your pot collapses while throwing?
options: C) Start over with new clay
quiz.explanation: Slowing the wheel reduces centrifugal force and lets you regain control.

quiz.q: What causes 'S' cracks in the base of a pot?
quiz.explanation: Compressing the base aligns clay particles and prevents S-cracks.

quiz.q: How can you fix a pot that is too dry to trim?
options: B) Spray with water and wait
quiz.explanation: Misting with water and waiting softens the clay enough to trim.

quiz.q: What is the best way to store clay to keep it workable?
options: B) In a sealed plastic bag
quiz.explanation: A sealed plastic bag retains moisture and prevents clay from drying out.

quiz.q: Why is it important to clean the wheel after throwing?
options: A) To prevent clay from hardening
quiz.explanation: Dried clay can damage the wheel head and make future throwing difficult.

quiz.q: What is a common sign that clay is too wet for throwing?
options: A) It feels sticky and slumps
quiz.explanation: Sticky, slumping clay lacks structure and won't hold shape.

quiz.q: What should you do if your pot wobbles on the wheel after throwing?
quiz.explanation: Gentle pressure on the high side can bring the pot back to center.

quiz.q: How can you prevent a rim from cracking during drying?
options: A) Dry it in the sun
quiz.explanation: Covering slows drying and reduces stress on the rim.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a needle tool?
quiz.explanation: A needle tool is used for marking, measuring, and testing thickness.

quiz.q: What is the recommended wall thickness for a large platter?
quiz.explanation: 1 cm provides strength for a large, flat piece without being too heavy.

quiz.q: What should you do if your trimming tool chatters?
options: B) Hold it firmly and spin slower
quiz.explanation: Chatter comes from vibration; slower speed and a firm grip reduce it.
